summary: Specifies a Telnet option that lets hosts exchange terminal speed information. Hosts that do so were expected to follow it. It was a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The TERMINAL-SPEED option lets Telnet hosts request and report terminal speeds. A reply gives the transmit and receive rates as two numbers separated by a comma.

subtitle: A Telnet option for exchanging a terminal's transmit and receive speeds.

tldr.problem: Some terminal-related display behavior depends on the terminal's bit rate, but a Telnet connection needs a way to carry that information.
tldr.mechanism: After negotiation, one side requests the information and the other replies with decimal transmit and receive speeds separated by a comma.
tldr.outcome: Hosts that exchange terminal speed information within Telnet are expected to follow this standard.

today: RFC 1079 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Terminal Speed Is Shared
sections.content:
Operating systems may track the speed of directly connected terminals and modems. Programs use that information for timing-dependent display work, such as choosing how many padding characters to send, and some interfaces adjust to fast or slow terminals.

This Telnet option makes similar speed information available across a network connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs can use a terminal's speed to time display output. The option carries that information across a Telnet connection.

sections.title: Negotiation and Requests
sections.content:
The TERMINAL-SPEED option has code 32. WILL indicates willingness to send speed information, while DO indicates willingness to receive it. The default is WON'T and DON'T, so no information is exchanged unless the option is negotiated.

After agreement, only the sender of DO may request the information. The sender of WILL supplies it, and may not send it without a request.
sections.plainLanguage: The hosts first agree to exchange speed information. Then the receiving side asks, and the sending side replies.

sections.title: Speed Format and Suggestions
sections.content:
A request uses IAC SB TERMINAL-SPEED SEND IAC SE, with SEND code 1. The response uses IAC SB TERMINAL-SPEED IS ... IAC SE, with IS code 0. The value is NVT ASCII decimal text: transmit speed, a comma, then receive speed, with no leading zeroes or extra characters.

The RFC suggests choosing the nearest allowed speed if a system supports only discrete rates. For padding, it suggests rounding up so that the padding is not too short.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply contains two decimal rates separated by a comma. If the exact rate is unavailable, the RFC suggests a safe nearby value for the task.

references.text: Solomon, M., and Wimmers, E., "Telnet Terminal Type Option", RFC 930, January 1985.
